chapters.title: Chapter 2: Theories of Exchange Rate Determination

lessons.title: Interest Rate Parity and the Logic of the Carry Trade

children.text: In Chapter 1 you saw a Bengaluru exporter book a 90-day forward at ₹83.90 when spot USD/INR was ₹83.00, and were told the gap was not a guess, it was arithmetic. This lesson supplies that arithmetic. It is called interest rate parity, and it is also the theory behind one of the most persistently profitable, and periodically catastrophic, trades in global finance: the carry trade.

body.text: Interest rate parity says the gap between a currency's forward and spot rate should exactly offset the interest rate difference between the two countries, so that no one can earn a riskless profit just by borrowing in one currency and investing in another.

children.text: Covered Interest Rate Parity: The No-Arbitrage Rule

markDefs.definition: A trade that would generate a certain, riskless profit with no capital of your own at stake, typically by exploiting a pricing inconsistency across two markets. Efficient markets are not supposed to leave these lying around for long.

children.text: Covered interest rate parity (CIP) is a no-

condition: if it did not hold, you could borrow in the low-interest-rate currency, convert it to the high-interest-rate currency, invest it there, lock in the forward rate to convert your proceeds back, and pocket a riskless profit with none of your own capital genuinely at risk. Banks and hedge funds watch for exactly this gap constantly, and their trading closes it almost as fast as it opens, which is why CIP holds very tightly in liquid, freely traded currency markets almost all the time.

body.caption: Covered interest rate parity: F is the forward rate, S the spot rate (both quoted as rupees per dollar), and i is each country's interest rate over the forward period.

children.text: Work through it with numbers. Say spot USD/INR is ₹83.00, India's one-year interest rate is 7%, and the US one-year rate is 5%. CIP says the one-year forward rate should be ₹83.00 x (1.07 / 1.05) = ₹84.58. Because India's interest rate is higher, the rupee trades at a forward discount and the dollar at a forward premium, you need more rupees to buy a dollar a year from now than you do today. This is not the market predicting rupee weakness, it is the arithmetic that prevents a riskless profit from the interest rate gap between the two countries.
Uncovered Interest Rate Parity: What Happens Without the Hedge

markDefs.definition: A well-documented empirical finding that high-interest-rate currencies tend not to depreciate by as much as uncovered interest rate parity predicts, and sometimes appreciate instead, making carry trades profitable on average over long periods, until they are not.

children.text: Uncovered interest rate parity (UIP) asks a different question: what should happen if you take the interest rate gap and do not hedge it forward at all? UIP predicts that the higher-interest-rate currency should be expected to depreciate, roughly by the size of the interest rate gap, so that an investor ends up with the same expected return whether they invest at home or abroad, once the currency move is factored in. Unlike CIP, which is an arbitrage condition that must hold, UIP is a theory about expectations, and it fails empirically far more often than it should, a persistent anomaly researchers call the
. That gap between what UIP predicts and what actually happens is precisely what makes the carry trade a real, recurring strategy rather than a theoretical curiosity.

body.caption: Covered vs. uncovered interest rate parity

cells: A no-arbitrage rule tying the forward rate to the interest rate gap
A theory about expected currency moves, with no hedge in place
Yes, very tightly, in liquid, freely traded currency markets
No, not reliably; this is the well-documented forward premium puzzle
Explains why forward rates differ from spot rates
Explains why the carry trade can be persistently, if riskily, profitable

children.text: The Carry Trade: Betting Against Uncovered Interest Rate Parity

A carry trade borrows in a low-interest-rate currency and invests, unhedged, in a higher-interest-rate currency, betting that UIP's prediction, that the higher-yielding currency should depreciate enough to erase the gain, will not fully play out. Take an FPI that borrows $1,000,000 at 5%, converts it to rupees at ₹83.00 spot, and invests in Indian government bonds yielding 7% for a year. If the rupee stays roughly flat, the trade earns close to the full 2% interest rate gap. If the rupee falls sharply instead, the currency loss can wipe out the interest gain entirely, and then some.

Run the numbers both ways. $1,000,000 converted at ₹83.00 becomes ₹8,30,00,000, which grows to ₹8,88,10,000 at 7% over the year. If the rupee is still at ₹83.00 when the FPI converts back, that is $1,070,000, a $20,000 profit, exactly the 2% differential, on $1,000,000 borrowed at 5%. But if the rupee weakens to ₹87.00 over the same year, converting back gives only about $1,020,805, against a $1,050,000 repayment, a loss of roughly $29,195. A rupee move of under 5% was enough to turn a clean 2% carry gain into a 2.9% loss.

body.title: Carry Trade Return on $1 Million, One-Year Horizon

body.text: A carry trade's profit comes almost entirely from the interest rate gap, a few percentage points a year. Its risk comes from the currency, which can move that much in a single volatile week. This asymmetry, small steady gains funded by rare but severe losses, is exactly what makes carry trades dangerous when they unwind all at once.

body.title: The Carry Trade: Reward vs. Risk

columns.label: What Draws Capital In
points: A steady, predictable interest rate gap, earned every day the trade is held
Works reliably as long as the funding currency stays weak and the target currency stays stable
Can be leveraged, small margin controlling a much larger position
Historically profitable on average across long stretches of calm markets

columns.label: What Can Wipe It Out
points: A sharp, sudden move in either currency erases months or years of accumulated gains
A surprise rate hike in the funding currency (the classic yen carry trade trigger) forces trades to unwind at once
Leverage that amplified gains amplifies losses just as fast
Crowded positioning means many traders exit simultaneously, worsening the currency move itself

body.title: Calculate the CIP Forward Rate
body.prompt: Spot USD/INR is ₹82.00. India's one-year interest rate is 6.5%, the US one-year rate is 4.5%. Using covered interest rate parity, what should the one-year forward USD/INR rate be?
body.explanation: F = 82.00 x (1.065 / 1.045) = 82.00 x 1.019139 = ₹83.57. India's higher rate means the rupee trades at a forward discount, the dollar costs more rupees a year out than it does today, purely to prevent a riskless arbitrage from the rate gap.

body.title: When the Carry Trade Unwinds
body.scenario: In early August 2024, the Bank of Japan raised interest rates unexpectedly after years of near-zero rates. Global investors who had borrowed cheap yen for years to fund higher-yielding positions elsewhere rushed to unwind those trades at once, the yen spiked sharply against major currencies and global equity markets, including Japan's own Nikkei, sold off hard within days.
body.prompt: Why does a single interest rate decision in Japan cause forced selling in unrelated markets around the world? What does this tell you about the risk in any carry trade funded by a currency everyone assumes will stay cheap indefinitely?
body.modelAnswer: A carry trade funded in yen is a short position in yen, borrowed and sold to fund something else. When the BOJ raises rates, two things happen together: the cost of servicing that yen loan rises, and the yen itself tends to strengthen as the interest rate gap that made it attractive to borrow narrows. Both effects hit the trade at once. Because so much global capital had put on similar yen-funded trades over years of near-zero Japanese rates, the unwind was not one fund quietly closing a position, it was a large share of the market trying to buy back yen and sell risk assets simultaneously, which itself pushed the yen up further and asset prices down further, a self-reinforcing spiral. The broader lesson: a carry trade's real risk is never just the currency pair you are watching, it is how many other traders are running the identical trade, and how violently a single central bank surprise can force them all to exit together.

points: Covered interest rate parity (CIP) is a no-arbitrage rule: the forward rate must offset the interest rate gap between two currencies, or a riskless profit would exist. It holds tightly in liquid markets almost all the time.

Uncovered interest rate parity (UIP) predicts the higher-interest-rate currency should depreciate by roughly the rate gap if left unhedged. It fails empirically far more often than it should, the forward premium puzzle.
A carry trade borrows in a low-interest-rate currency and invests unhedged in a higher-interest-rate one, effectively betting that UIP's predicted depreciation will not fully materialise.

The carry trade's profit is a small, steady interest rate gap; its risk is a sudden currency move that can erase months of gains in days, especially when funding-currency interest rates rise unexpectedly.

Crowded carry trades unwind violently because many participants are forced to exit the same position at once, as the 2024 yen carry trade unwind showed, turning a single central bank decision into a global market event.
